title: Chapter 56: Fire Under Glass, Part 2 of 5: The Last Bid
html:
The man at the top of the back stair was perhaps nineteen.
Corin saw him as they came round the last turn. A thin boy in a gray Inquisition coat too big for him, with a long gray truncheon in one hand and a lantern in the other, standing in the little square landing at the top of the green steps with his back against a door. The smoke was rolling round his boots. His face was white. His eyes were running with it. And he was shaking so hard that the light of his lantern jumped about the walls like a moth.
He saw Mrs. Pratt and lifted the truncheon.
"Stop there," he said. His voice cracked. "Nobody up. Orders. The Inquisitor's orders. Nobody—"
Mrs. Pratt did not stop.
She came up the last three steps with the cleaver in her hand and her great red arms bare to the elbow, and she did not lift the cleaver at all. She just walked into him. The way a cart walks into a gate. She put her free hand flat on his chest and leaned, and he went back against the door with a thump, and the truncheon fell out of his hand and went rattling down the stair past Corin's feet.
"How old are you?" said Mrs. Pratt.
The boy stared at her.
"Nineteen," he said.
"Got a mother?"
"Yes."
"Then go home to her," said Mrs. Pratt. "Go on. Down those stairs and out of the gate and home. Your Inquisitor's going to burn this house down round your ears, boy, and you with it, and he'll never think of you again. Go home."
The boy looked at her. At the cleaver. At the smoke.
Then he looked at Corin. A lame old cellarman with a stick. And something in his white face gave way.
He went. Down the stair, past them both, pressing himself flat to the wall, with his lantern swinging. They heard his boots go round the turns, faster and faster, and then they did not.
Mrs. Pratt opened the door.
The heat came through it like a fist.
Corin had been in fires before. He had been in the loft over Hollis's shop, in the autumn, when it burned with all the jars in it and they flew out of the windows like birds. He had been in the wet house. But he had never felt heat like this. It came out of the doorway in one great slow solid wave, and hit him in the face, and went down into his chest when he breathed, and he felt Vespera's paint on his cheeks go soft. He put up his arm. He put his face into the crook of it, into Fenton's coat, and breathed through the cloth.
And went through the door.
He was in the gallery.
He knew it. He had seen it from below, pouring wine for the Duke at the eleventh bell. The gallery ran all the way round the inside of the dome, high up, under the glass, like the rim round the top of a cup. It was a long curved walk with a carved railing on one side and curtains on the other. Heavy velvet curtains, deep violet, Vivienne's color, hung on brass rings from a brass rail, and behind them, Remy had said, were the little private rooms of the Fourth Tier, where the lords who had been asked could sit with their wine and watch the floor below without being seen. And behind those, her rooms. The Lady's own.
The curtains on this side were burning.
Not all of them. Not yet. But the two nearest the door had caught, low down, at the hem, and the fire was going up them the way a fire goes up dry grass. Fast and bright and quiet. Corin saw it go up the velvet in a long yellow tongue while he watched, and reach the brass rail, and run along it, and drop onto the next curtain, and start up that one too.
And beyond the railing, the dome.
He went to the railing. He did not mean to. His feet took him. He went to it with his arm over his face and his stick sliding on the polished boards, and put his gloved hand on the carved wood, and looked over.
And saw.
The floor of the Memory Bourse was forty feet below him. The great round floor, black and white, like a chessboard, with the brass box in the middle on its iron pillar. And round the brass box, the hole. The ring of black squares that had sunk at a quarter to midnight, like a lid into a well. It had not come back up. It was still down. A great black ring of nothing round the brass box, twelve paces across, with smoke pouring up out of it, gray and thick and lit from below by a dull red glow.
The cold room, Corin thought. The shelves. The jars.
Gideon.
Round the edge of the hole, the long glass tables. The ring of them, where the lots had been laid out all evening on plum velvet, each with its little white card. Some were still standing. Some had been knocked over, and the glass had broken, and the vials and jars had gone rolling across the black and white floor in all directions, shining, like marbles spilled out of a bag. People were walking on them. Treading on them. And where a jar broke under a heel, a little puff of light went up, gray or blue or gold, and hung for a moment in the smoky air, and then faded.
And the people.
There were hundreds of them. The lords and ladies of the Hill, in their silks and velvets and feathers and masks, pressed together in a great frightened mass on the black and white floor between the tables and the walls. They were being herded. Corin could see it from up here. Like sheep in a pen. By men in gray. Inquisition men, in gray coats, with truncheons, forty or fifty of them, in a line, walking slowly forward, pressing the crowd toward the great bronze doors at the front of the dome. And at the bronze doors, which stood wide open now with the night and the torches of Exchange Street beyond them, more men in gray. And one in the middle of them.
Kross.
He was standing just inside the doors. On a chair. Somebody had brought him a chair from one of the tables, a gilt chair with plum velvet on the seat, and he was standing on it, a little above the crowd, in his long plain gray coat, with his hat on and his hands behind his back. And as each lord and lady came to the doors, pushed by the men behind, they had to pass him. Right under him. Close enough to touch. And he looked down at each of them. Just looked. For a moment. And then nodded, and they were let through, out into the torchlight and the night.
He's going to walk them out of those doors one at a time and look at every one of their faces.
Oren had been right.
Some of them had taken off their masks. Corin could see the masks on the floor round the chair, a little heap of them, white and gold and silver and black, feathered and jeweled, dropped there. As if the lords had thought that Kross would let them pass quicker if they showed him their faces. As if they had thought it would help.
Corin looked for Lyra.
He looked for her the way you look for one star in a sky full of them. All across the black and white floor. Through the smoke. Through the crowd. A gray gown. A white mask. Hair cut short and ragged and combed flat. The Duke of Marrow's dove-gray silk beside her, and his ten rings.
He could not see her.
He looked again. Slower. Starting at the bronze doors and going round, the way you search a room, the way he had been taught at the Ministry, a strip at a time. The doors. The chair. The heap of masks. The crowd, one face at a time. The line of gray coats. The tables. The broken glass. The hole.
The hole.
There was a girl at the edge of the hole.
On the far side of it. Across the black ring of smoke from where he stood. Alone. Standing quite still at the very edge of the black squares, where the floor stopped and the drop began, with the smoke pouring up past her out of the red glow below. Not in the crowd. Not being herded. Standing apart from all of it, with her back to the bronze doors and to Kross, looking down.
In a gray gown. With a white mask in her hand, not on her face.
Counting.
He could not hear her. He could not see her lips from here. But he knew. The way she stood. The way her head was a little on one side, and her free hand was down by her skirt, and the fingers of it were moving. Tapping. On the gray silk. One. Two. Three.
Tell her to keep counting.
She was counting the people coming up out of the hole.
Because there were people coming up. Corin saw them now. Out of the smoke. Out of the black ring, from below, from the cold room. Porters. Men in plum aprons with their faces black, climbing up out of the hole by the iron chains of the lift, which hung down into it at the four corners of the brass box's pillar, hand over hand, coughing. Three of them. Four. A woman in a white cap. They came up over the edge onto the black and white floor and lay there, and the men in gray did not go to them, and Lyra stood at the edge above them with her white mask in her hand, counting.
Waiting for one more.
For a lame man with a black case.
She did not know he had gone out by the chute. She did not know the case was with Oren, halfway to Saint Bride's by now. She did not know anything. She only knew that the floor had sunk at a quarter to midnight, and that he had been under it, and that the lift had come up at five to twelve with Lot 41 on its velvet tray, and the Weigher had called it, and the bids had gone into the box, and at the twelfth bell the Lady had opened the box and—
And what?
Corin looked at the brass box.
It stood on its iron pillar in the middle of the hole, alone, with the smoke going up all round it. Its lid was open. And on the flat top of the pillar beside it, where the lift had stopped, there was the velvet tray.
It was empty.
The decoy was gone.
And as Corin looked at the empty tray, something moved at the edge of his eye. On the far side of the dome. Away to the right of the bronze doors, by the wall. Where there was a small plain door in the curve of the wall, a door you would hardly see unless you were looking for it, with a porter on each side of it in plum.
The garden door.
It was open.
And a man was going out through it.
Not a lord. Not a porter. A small neat man in a plain dark coat, with his back very straight, and his head a little bent, and something held carefully in both arms against his chest. Something black. With silver at the corners.
The porters on each side of the garden door did not stop him. And there was a man in gray at the door too, Corin saw now. One of Kross's. Standing just beside it. And the man in gray did not stop him either. He stepped back. He stepped back, and turned his face away, the way you turn your face away from something you have been told not to see.
And the small neat man went out through the garden door into the dark with the black case in his arms.
Corin knew the back of that head. He had sat across from it on Saturday night and asked it three questions.
Lucian.
Lucian, who had told the stair Corin's route on purpose. Who had a black book with a page in it for Midwinter. Ninth bell. The Bourse. Masked. By the garden door. Who carried another man's case with four hollows in it, and put another man's card in the brass box.
The Archon's card had won.
And the Archon had already gone. Gone out by the garden door, at the first blow of the ram, before the lamps began to burst, Corin would have bet his life on it. Gone out quietly in his black half-mask and his black gloves, while the lords were still turning to scream. And had left his secretary behind to collect what he had bought.
And Kross's man at the door had stepped back and looked away.
Whoever buys it will not live to open it.
Nobody would open that case. Not ever. There was nothing in it, and a pin set in solid where the clasp should be, and you would need an axe. And when they took an axe to it, in some quiet room somewhere, and found it empty—
Corin did not finish the thought.
Because right above him, so close he felt the wind of it on the back of his neck, one of the brass Ash lamps on its long chain from the iron ribs of the dome went white, and hissed, and burst.
Fire Under Glass
It was not like a gun. Mrs. Pratt had been wrong about that.
A gun goes off with a bang and then it is over. This was not over. The lamp went white, and the white went into Corin's eyes so that for a moment he could see nothing else, and there was a sound like a great sheet of glass being torn in half. And then the brass case of the lamp came apart. Not into pieces. It opened, the way a flower opens, its brass sides peeling back on their hinges, very fast. And out of it came the light.
Not fire. Not at first. Light. Pale and blue and cold, the cold steady blue of the Crescent Gas that burned in the street lamps on the Hill. It came pouring out of the burst lamp in a great slow cloud, the way water pours out of a broken jug. And it did not fall. It spread. It went out into the hot smoky air under the dome, all round the lamp, in a ball, growing, twisting, folding over on itself, the way the light in the jars in the cold room had folded over on itself. Only faster. Much faster. Wild.
And it touched him.
It came down over the railing like a fog and touched his face and his hands and went in at his eyes and his mouth when he breathed, and he was—
—a woman in a kitchen with flour on her hands and a baby on her hip, singing, and the window open, and the smell of rain—
—a boy on a wall, kicking his heels, with an apple, and the sun in his eyes, and his brother calling from the field below—
—an old man at a grave with his hat in his hands, and the wind in the grass, and the name on the stone that was his wife's—
—a girl, a little girl, in a white dress, at a window, waiting for somebody who was not coming—
Corin fell against the railing.
He did not know he had fallen. He was holding on to the carved wood with both hands and his stick was gone, rattling away along the boards, and his face was wet. And the memories were going through him. Not his. Not anybody's he knew. Strangers. Dozens of them, a hundred, the whole of what had been poured into that one brass lamp to make it burn blue for a year. Pouring through him and out the other side, like water through a sieve. Faster than he could see them. A wedding. A fever. A ship. A hand. A song. A dog. A death. A field. A face. A face. A face.
The Ash of them.
He was a harvester. He had been born, or made, with the door in him that let it in. And every man and woman in this dome who did not have that door, who had only felt a breath of warm wind as the cloud went over them, was screaming. He could hear them. Below him, on the black and white floor, as the cloud of cold blue light came down over the crowd, he heard the screaming change. It went from fear to something else. Something much worse. The sound people make when they are suddenly someone else, for a moment, a hundred other people, and do not know where they are.
BOY.
Malakor.
Not a shout this time. A voice like an iron bar, driven straight down through the middle of him.
Shut it. Shut the door. You know how. You've done it a thousand times. On the wet stair. In the attic. Shut it. NOW.
Corin shut it.
He did not know how. He had never known how. It was not a thing you knew. It was like shutting your eyes, or swallowing, a thing your body did. He found the place in himself where the door was, behind his left ear, under the place where Malakor lived, and he put both hands on it, inside himself, and pushed. And the door went shut. Not all the way. A crack of it stayed open, and through the crack the strangers' memories still came, thin, like a draft under a door. But the flood of it stopped.
He was on his knees on the gallery boards with his forehead against the carved railing. Breathing.
Good, said Malakor. Good. Now get up. It's going to catch.
It caught.
The cloud of cold blue light under the dome, spreading and twisting, touched the burning curtains of the gallery. And where it touched them, it changed.
Corin saw it happen. He would see it for the rest of his life, in the place where he kept the things he could not forget. The blue light touched the yellow flame on the velvet, and for one moment the two of them seemed to look at each other. And then the blue went white. Not the white of the lamp before it burst. A worse white. A white like the middle of a forge. And it went out along the cloud, all through it, from the place where it had touched the flame, in one great silent rush, like a fire running along a trail of lamp oil. And the whole cloud, the whole ball of strangers' memories hanging in the air under the dome, went up.
It did not burn. It flashed. There was no other word for it. One great white flash, filling the dome from the floor to the glass, so bright that Corin saw the bones of his own hands through the white cotton of his gloves. And with it, the heat. Not a wave this time. A blow. As if the air itself had struck him. It knocked him back from the railing and laid him flat on the gallery boards and went over him, and he heard his own hair crackle, and smelled it.
And then it was gone.
And the fire was everywhere.
He lay on his back on the boards and looked up, and the whole inside of the dome was alight. Every curtain in the gallery, all the way round, on every side, was burning. The great violet velvet curtains, a hundred of them, hanging from their brass rails, every one of them a long sheet of yellow flame from top to bottom. The carved railings were burning. The gilt chairs in the little private rooms behind the curtains were burning. And above it all, the glass of the dome had gone black with smoke, and through the black, between the iron ribs, the orange of the fire shone up and back and down again, so that the whole great shell of glass seemed to be breathing fire.
And the lamps.
The other lamps. The ninety-nine others, hanging on their long brass chains from the iron ribs. One after another. Going white. Bursting. Opening like flowers. Pouring out their slow blue clouds of strangers' memories into the hot air. And every cloud, as it touched the fire, going up in its own white flash.
Crack. White. Flash. Heat.
Crack. White. Flash. Heat.
Like a string of crackers at a fair.
Corin rolled over. He got onto his hands and knees. His stick was gone, he did not know where. He got hold of the railing, where the carving had not caught yet, and pulled himself up it on his good leg, and looked over again.
The floor of the dome was a field of fire.
The long glass tables round the hole had gone up. The plum velvet on them had caught in the first flash, and burned, and now the glass of the tables themselves was cracking in the heat, crack and crack, and the vials and jars that had been laid out on them, the lots that had not been sold, were bursting one after another. Each one with its own little white flash. Each one with its own small burst of somebody's life, going up into the smoke. A summer afternoon. River, boat, a girl's laugh. Gone. The smell of a bakery, early. Gone.
And the people.
They were not being herded now. There was nothing to herd. The great frightened mass of the lords and ladies of the Hill had broken apart in the first white flash like a wave on a rock, and now they were running. Everywhere. In every direction. Screaming. With their silks and feathers burning. Corin saw a lady in a gown of green satin run past the end of a burning table with her great tall hair alight on her head, a column of yellow flame, like a candle. He saw a man in a black mask beating at another man's back with his bare hands. He saw a girl no older than Lyra sitting quite still on the black and white floor with her mask in her lap, among the broken glass, looking up at the burning dome with her mouth open, not moving, while the people ran past her on both sides.
And the men in gray.
They were not running. That was the thing. That was the thing Corin would remember. In all that fire and screaming, the men in gray were not running. They had pulled back. All of them. All forty or fifty. In a neat gray line, all the way back to the walls, to the doors. To the bronze doors at the front, and the garden door at the side, and the doors of the gallery stairs. And they were standing in front of the doors. In twos and threes. Very still. With their truncheons in their hands.
Not letting anybody out.
No. That was not right. He looked again. They were letting people out. But slowly. One at a time. Looking at each face. The way Kross had looked, from his chair. A lord came running to the bronze doors with his coat on fire, and two men in gray caught him, and held him, and looked at his face, and then threw him out into the night like a sack. A lady in white came screaming, and they held her, and looked, and let her go.
They were still looking.
With the dome burning over their heads, they were still looking at every face.
And on his gilt chair just inside the bronze doors, with the fire roaring all round him and the smoke pouring out over his head into Exchange Street, Silas Kross had not moved. He stood on the chair with his hands behind his back and his hat on his head, quite still, quite calm, and watched the Memory Bourse burn. The way a man watches a bonfire on a winter night. With his face lit orange. Waiting.
For one face.
Corin looked at the hole.
The girl in the gray gown was still there.
She had not moved. She had not run. She was standing at the very edge of the black ring of nothing, on the far side of it, with the fire all round her and the smoke pouring up past her out of the red glow below, with her white mask still in her hand. And she was still counting. He could see her free hand, by her skirt, moving. Tapping. The burning tables on either side of her. The running people. The bursting jars. And she stood in the middle of it all and looked down into the hole, and counted, and waited, for a man who was not going to come up out of it.
She doesn't know, thought Corin. She doesn't know I came out.
She thinks I'm still down there.
She's not going to leave.
Above him, from somewhere high up in the black of the glass, there came a long, deep, slow groan. Iron. Bending.
And then a crack. Sharp and high and very loud. Like ice breaking on a river.
And a single pane of glass, as big as a door, came loose from the dome, high up near the top, between two iron ribs, and fell. Corin watched it fall. It turned over and over in the air, slowly, catching the firelight, like a leaf. Forty feet. Fifty. And hit the black and white floor beside the brass box, at the edge of the hole, twenty paces from where she stood, and burst into a thousand pieces, and the pieces went out across the floor like spray.
She did not even look round.
Corin let go of the railing.
And went to find the stairs.
